These findings support further evaluation of segmentation-guided multimodal MRI analysis for preoperative molecular subtype assessment.

articles.title: Edge-Aware and Wavelet-Enhanced Detection Transformer for Esophageal Cancer Screening in Barium Meal Images.
articles.abstract: Early detection of esophageal cancer through non-invasive barium meal imaging is critical for improving patient outcomes, yet the weak lesion boundaries, subtle textures, and high background noise in these images pose fundamental challenges for automated detection. Current methods face two technical bottlenecks: backbone networks lose fragile edge information during downsampling, while feature pyramids introduce detail loss and spatial misalignment during upsampling, together causing high miss rates for superficial lesions and imprecise boundary localization. Here, we present EWE-DETR, a detection framework that addresses these limitations through two complementary innovations. First, an Edge-Aware Partial-Attention backbone (EAP) employs parallel edge and semantic branches to simultaneously capture local boundary details and global anatomical context, preserving lesion edges from the earliest layers. Second, a Wavelet-Enhanced Edge-Semantic Feature Pyramid Network (WES-FPN) uses wavelet transforms for frequency-preserving upsampling and cross-layer edge injection to eliminate traditional upsampling artifacts. Across 10 matched random seeds on the EC-BSID dataset, EWE-DETR achieved an mAP50 of 86.06% ± 0.19% and an F1 score of 83.20% ± 0.60%. Compared with JS-DETR, the closest-performing comparator in terms of mAP50, EWE-DETR yielded higher point estimates across all core detection metrics, including a 7.04-percentage-point improvement in precision. These findings support further evaluation of EWE-DETR as a candidate computer-aided screening tool; however, given the single-center retrospective design of this study, they do not establish its direct deployability in primary-care hospitals or across different imaging devices.

articles.title: Predictive Nomogram for High Ki-67 Expression using Contrast-Enhanced Ultrasound of Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Identifying reliable prognostic factors for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) is challenging, thereby complicating treatment and follow-up decisions. The aim of this study was to develop and validate a contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS)-based nomogram to predict high Ki-67 expression in ccRCC. This retrospective study analysed 312 patients from two centres (training, n = 212; validation, n = 100) who underwent preoperative CEUS. Postoperative pathology confirmed ccRCC. Immunohistochemistry assessed Ki-67 expression and CD34-positive microvascular density (CD34+MVD). A nomogram was developed using multivariate logistic regression and validated based on the area under the curve (AUC). Predictive performance was compared with tumour-node-metastasis (TNM) staging and World Health Organisation/International Society of Urological Pathology (WHO/ISUP) grading using the DeLong test. Spearman's correlation coefficients were compared among CD34+MVD, WHO/ISUP grade, and Ki-67 expression. Significant predictors of high Ki-67 expression included tumour diameter ≥ 3.85 cm (odds ratio [OR]: 1.525, 95% confidence interval: 1.054-2.205), washout time ≤ 34.7 s (OR: 0.942, 95% Cl: 0.911-0.975), and necrosis ≥ 9.158% (OR: 1.105, 95% Cl: 1.021-1.195). The nomogram achieved an AUC of 0.858 (training set) and 0.810 (validation set), outperforming TNM staging (AUC: 0.733) and WHO/ISUP grading (AUC: 0.761). Ki-67 expression correlated negatively with CD34+MVD (r = -0.632) and positively with WHO/ISUP grading (r=0.620), whereas CD34+MVD expression was negatively correlated with WHO/ISUP grading (r = -0.607). The CEUS-based nomogram demonstrated superior predictive accuracy for high Ki-67 expression compared with TNM staging and WHO/ISUP grading, supporting its potential for personalised treatment and more precise follow-up surveillance programmes.

articles.title: Quantitative imaging-pathology correlation in nodular fasciitis and diagnostic discrimination from sarcoma.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To investigate associations between key magnetic resonance imaging features of nodular fasciitis (NF) and quantitative histopathologic biomarkers, and to evaluate whether their integration provides complementary information for differentiating NF from soft tissue sarcoma (STS) in diagnostically equivocal settings. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study included 128 patients with NF and 133 with STS who underwent preoperative 3-T MRI between May 2023 and June 2025. Two blinded musculoskeletal radiologists independently evaluated predefined imaging features, including fascial tail sign, T2 heterogeneity score, enhancement pattern, perilesional edema, and mean/minimum apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC). Histopathology quantified cellular density, collagen content, and myxoid degeneration. Imaging-pathology correlations were assessed using Spearman analysis and multivariable regression. Diagnostic performance of MRI-only, pathology-only, and combined models was evaluated using logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic (ROC), area under the curve (AUC) analysis, calibration, decision curve analysis, and bootstrap validation. RESULTS: T2 heterogeneity correlated positively with myxoid degeneration (ρ = 0.52) and negatively with collagen content (ρ = -0.28) (p < 0.001). Mean ADC correlated inversely with cellular density (ρ = -0.63, p < 0.001). Mean ADC was significantly higher in NF than STS (p < 0.001). The combined model outperformed MRI alone (AUC, 0.96 vs 0.89) and demonstrated greater net clinical benefit. Bootstrap validation confirmed stable performance (mean AUC, 0.960; 95% confidence interval, 0.938-0.978). CONCLUSION: Imaging features of NF were associated with underlying stromal and cellular substrates. Integrating imaging features with quantitative pathology biomarkers may support radiology-pathology concordance assessment in selected diagnostically equivocal cases. KEY POINTS: Question How can we improve radiology-pathology concordance and reduce interpretative variability for NF cases presenting with suspicious, diagnostically equivocal magnetic resonance imaging findings? Findings T2 heterogeneity and diffusion measurements are associated with stromal composition and cellularity, while predefined MRI features demonstrated substantial-to-excellent inter-reader agreement. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

articles.title: Large language model-based simplification of breast imaging reports: a prospective multicentre study with 2965 patient-based evaluations.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To compare patient perceptions of radiologist-written and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated simplifications of breast imaging reports in terms of simplicity, comprehensibility, empathy, and overall preference. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective multicentre survey-based study, 10 anonymized breast imaging reports (5 ultrasound, 5 mammography; one BI-RADS category 1-5 per modality) were simplified by ChatGPT-4 within a 50-word limit. After assessment by a panel of 20 physicians, paired radiologist-written and AI-generated reports were evaluated by 314 patients (2965 evaluations) who rated simplicity, comprehensibility, and empathy on a 5-point Likert scale and indicated their preferred report. The origin of each report was concealed, and each pair was presented in randomized order. Univariable and multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression analyses were performed to identify factors associated with preferring AI-generated reports. RESULTS: AI-generated reports were preferred in 63.3% (1876/2965) of evaluations. High simplicity and comprehensibility scores (4-5) were more frequently assigned to AI reports than to radiologist-written reports (70.0% vs 43.4% and 68.1% vs 40.4%, respectively). In multivariable analysis, higher comprehensibility was the strongest predictor in both directions: higher comprehensibility of AI-generated reports increased the odds of preferring AI (score 4: adjusted OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.08-3.23, p = 0.025), while higher comprehensibility of radiologist-written reports reduced them (score 4: adjusted OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.29-0.69, p < 0.001). Preference for AI-generated reports showed a non-significant trend toward increase with educational level. CONCLUSION: AI-generated breast imaging reports were preferred by most patients and perceived as clearer, supporting a complementary and supervised use of AI-generated summaries. KEY POINTS: Question Patients increasingly access their own radiology reports, yet standard radiologist-written reports are often difficult to understand, highlighting the need for patient-friendly alternatives. Findings In this study, AI-generated breast imaging reports were preferred by patients in 63.3% of evaluations, with comprehensibility emerging as the strongest predictor of preference. CRITICAL RELEVANCE STATEMENT: AI-generated breast imaging reports were preferred by most patients and received higher ratings for simplicity and comprehensibility than radiologist-written reports, supporting a supervised and complementary use of AI-generated summaries in clinical breast imaging.

articles.title: Clinical validation of Node-RADS for nodal staging in colon cancer: a retrospective study of 360 patients.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to assess the effectiveness of the Node Reporting and Data System version 1.0 (Node-RADS 1.0) for preoperative evaluation of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in colon cancer and to benchmark its diagnostic performance against conventional CT-based size criteria. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study enrolled patients who underwent radical resection for colon cancer at Shantou Central Hospital between January 2015 and January 2019. All patients received radical resection followed by histopathological evaluation of regional lymph nodes. Preoperative computed tomography (CT) images were independently reviewed by two experienced radiologists using the Node-RADS scoring system. Inter-observer agreement was assessed, and diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. RESULTS: A total of 360 patients were included. Lymph node positivity was associated with several CT features, including nodal size, internal heterogeneity, necrosis, margin characteristics, fatty hilum status, and the Node-RADS score (all p < 0.05). The Node-RADS score demonstrated the highest diagnostic performance (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.835, 95% CI: 0.792-0.871) with an optimal cutoff of ≥3, good inter-observer reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) = 0.962), and higher discriminative ability than the conventional 10-mm size criterion (AUC 0.546; p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: In this large retrospective cohort, contrast-enhanced CT-based Node-RADS demonstrated reliable diagnostic performance for preoperative assessment of LNM in colon cancer and outperformed the conventional size-based criterion. The good inter-observer agreement further supports the reproducibility and clinical feasibility of Node-RADS in routine clinical practice. KEY POINTS: Question Can CT-based Node-RADS overcome the low sensitivity and underestimation of nodal metastasis associated with the conventional 10-mm short-axis criterion in preoperative colon cancer staging? Findings In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases. Critical relevance statement In 360 patients, Node-RADS at ≥3 achieved an AUC of 0.835, 96.6% sensitivity, and good interobserver agreement, outperforming the 10-mm criterion with fewer missed metastases.

articles.title: Simplifying CT/MRI LI-RADS v2018 Maintains Diagnostic Performance: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) diagnostic algorithm assesses hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) probability of liver observations in high-risk individuals, but complexity may limit its adoption. PURPOSE: To evaluate whether LI-RADS v2018 can be simplified without impairing diagnostic performance by removing threshold growth (TG) and reducing size cut-offs. STUDY TYPE: Retrospective meta-analysis. POPULATION: Eight thousand five hundred eighty-two patients (mean age: 59 ± 11 years; 6610 male) at risk for HCC with CT/MRI (986 CT, 6554 MRI, and 1042 CT/MRI). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: Field strength: 1.5T and 3.0T; sequences varied by institution per LI-RADS technical requirements. ASSESSMENT: LI-RADS v2018 using major features only was compared with seven simplifications removing TG and/or applying single size cut-offs (≥ 10, ≥ 15, and ≥ 20 mm) in individual participant data (IPD) of 64 studies (29 institutions, 11 countries) from the LI-RADS Living Systematic Review and IPD Meta-analysis Project. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. STATISTICAL TESTS: Summary receiver operating characteristic curves estimated area under the curve (AUC) across LR-3 to LR-5; LR-5 sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value (PPV) were estimated using a one-step bivariate mixed-effects model. Differences were assessed by cluster bootstrap. p < 0.05 indicated significance, uncorrected for multiple comparisons. RESULTS: Nine thousand four hundred six observations were included. Excluding TG with a 10-mm cut-off showed AUC similar to LI-RADS v2018 (0.80 vs. 0.81, p = 0.44) and significantly higher LR-5 sensitivity (73.8% vs. 71.8%) with similar specificity (72.5% vs. 73.7%, p = 0.13) and PPV (97.8% vs. 97.8%, p = 0.73). Removing TG with 15-mm and 20-mm cut-offs had significantly lower AUC than v2018 (-0.03 [95% CI: -0.041, -0.019]; -0.043 [-0.054, -0.032], respectively) and sensitivity (-13.2% [95% CI: -14.5%, -12.0%]; -30.1% [-31.7%, -28.5%], respectively). Of the 64 studies, 17 had low-risk of bias, and 56 had low applicability concerns. CONCLUSION: Simplifying LI-RADS v2018 by removing TG and using a 10-mm size cut-off preserved diagnostic table AUC while improving LR-5 sensitivity without loss of specificity or PPV. PROTOCOL REGISTRATION: Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/cjwgp). EVIDENCE LEVEL: 3. TECHNICAL EFFICIENCY: Stage 2.

articles.title: MRI-Derived Lymph Node Characteristics for Risk Stratification of Distant Metastasis in Locoregionally Advanced Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: MRI-derived nodal features may improve prognostication beyond TNM staging, but distant-metastasis risk models remain limited. PURPOSE: To develop and internally validate an MRI model for distant metastasis prediction in locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma (LA-NPC). STUDY TYPE: Retrospective. POPULATION: One thousand five-hundred and forty-one patients with LA-NPC (1103 men and 438 women; mean age, 48 ± 12 years) were split into a training set (n = 1079) and an internal validation set (n = 462). FIELD STRENGTH/SEQUENCE: 3.0-T MRI using axial T1-weighted turbo spin-echo, axial T2-weighted short-tau inversion recovery, diffusion-weighted imaging (b = 0 and 800 s/mm2) with apparent diffusion coefficient maps, and multiplanar fat-suppressed contrast-enhanced T1-weighted turbo spin-echo. ASSESSMENT: Extranodal extension (ENE), cervical lymph node necrosis (CNN), nodal size, regional lymph node density (RLND), nodal laterality, and clinical variables were assessed. Recursive partitioning analysis (RPA) defined risk groups, which were combined with T and N categories in a nomogram. STATISTICAL TESTS: Cox analyses were performed in training. Performance was assessed by the concordance index (C-index), 3-year time-dependent receiver operating characteristic analysis, and calibration. Two-sided p < 0.05 indicated significance. RESULTS: ENE Grade 3 (HR, 1.92; 95% CI, 1.20-3.07), CNN Grades 3-4 (HR, 2.65; 95% CI, 1.46-4.81), and RLND (per-unit increase: HR, 1.92; 95% CI, 1.29-2.88) were independently associated with shorter distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS). The multivariable model C-index was 0.766 (95% CI, 0.721-0.811). RPA assigned 491, 524, and 64 patients to low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, with 3-year DMFS rates of 97.53%, 89.90%, and 60.83%, respectively. Nomogram 3-year AUCs were 0.777 (95% CI, 0.725-0.828) in training and 0.728 (95% CI, 0.645-0.810) in validation; the difference was nonsignificant (p = 0.333). Mean absolute calibration errors were 0.009 and 0.012, respectively. DATA CONCLUSION: MRI-derived nodal features enabled DMFS risk stratification, and the internally validated nomogram showed discrimination and calibration. EVIDENCE LEVEL: 4. TECHNICAL EFFICACY: Stage 2.

articles.title: Assessing effects of low-dose CT attenuation correction on quantification and image quality on a LAFOV PET system with a modified NEMA-IQ phantom.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Over the past decades, efforts have been directed toward increasing the sensitivity of PET systems to enable low-dose PET imaging and shorter scan times. The Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT scanner (Siemens Healthineers, Knoxville, TN, USA) combines an increased solid angle coverage with time of flight, enabling a significant reduction in administered activity. To fully benefit from low-dose PET imaging, the dose of the CT scan should ideally also be reduced. PURPOSE: The CT radiation dose can be reduced by lowering the tube voltage and exposure as well as by the use of tin filtration. Reducing the CT dose must be carefully aligned with any impact that changing CT image quality and quantitative metrics may have on the PET quantification, for example via linear attenuation coefficients. We evaluate the impact of low-dose CT protocols on the PET quantification in soft-tissue-like and bone-equivalent materials using a customized phantom. METHODS: The phantom was assembled out of a NEMA-IQ phantom, several layers of saline and two bovine long bones, to simulate a patient positioned with arms down. A 10-min PET scan with 47 different accompanying CT scans was acquired. The CT tube voltage and exposure were varied between 70  k V  to  140  k V  , with and without tin filtration, and 7  mAs  to  400  mAs  , respectively. The effect of the different CT parameters on the PET image quality and quantitative accuracy was assessed via several quantitative metrics, including standardized uptake value (SUV) and signal-to-noise ratio, along with the CT dose length product (DLP). RESULTS: The recorded DLP values suggest that using all tube voltages except 140  k V  combined with exposures in the range of 7  m A s  to  30  m A s  , can result in dose savings of ≥ 80  %  compared to a typical clinical protocol ( 120  k V  , 50  mAs  ). Compared to this typical protocol, HU differed more in bone ( 10  %  to  40  %  difference) than in soft tissue ( 1  %  to  30  %  difference), and more streak artefacts and photon starvation were seen when configuring low tube voltages and exposures, with an accompanying increase in CT noise. The observed artefacts were transferred with low intensity to the PET images via the attenuation map. The SUV mean  remained within 2  %  of the SUV mean  of the typical clinical protocol for most tested protocols. The presence of artefacts in the CT images had a bigger impact on PET quantification in both soft tissue and bone ( SUV mean  difference of 10  %  to  20  %  ) than any difference in HU. Protocols that resulted in artefacts showed an increased inaccuracy in attenuation correction and scatter estimation, as assessed via the "lung" residual error (up to 10  %  to  20  %  increase). CONCLUSIONS: Even for low-dose CT protocols, PET quantification remained consistent in all NEMA-IQ spheres for many materials. Beam hardening and photon starvation in the CT image are likely to occur in specific body regions such as hips, shoulders or the abdomen for an arms-down scan and these effects had a bigger impact on the quantification than any difference in HU in both soft tissue and bone. This therefore should be considered when selecting suitable CT imaging parameters.

articles.title: Gaussian process regression of HDR prostate biopsy dose for improved modelling of localization-induced uncertainty.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Biopsy-level dose interpretation after high-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy is limited by localization uncertainty, and separate voxelwise Monte Carlo summaries do not explicitly account for the axial spatial correlation present along a biopsy core. PURPOSE: To develop and internally evaluate a biopsy-level Gaussian process regression framework for assigning along-core high-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy dose under localization uncertainty, and to test whether explicit modelling of axial spatial correlation improves uncertainty characterization relative to voxelwise Monte Carlo summaries treated independently. METHODS: We analyzed 27 MR-informed, transrectal-ultrasound (TRUS)-guided transperineal template biopsies from 15 patients treated with high-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy. For each biopsy voxel, Monte Carlo localization perturbations were propagated to generate dose summaries and voxel-specific variances. Biopsy-specific empirical semivariograms were fitted with candidate covariance kernels, and ordinary-mean heteroscedastic Gaussian process posteriors were computed along each core. Internal evaluation included latent-profile residual diagnostics, kernel-sensitivity analysis, and blocked cross-validation using contiguous held-out axial segments scored on held-out points only. RESULTS: For the selected baseline kernel, Matérn ν = 1.5  , the across-biopsy median voxel-averaged standard deviation was 6.91 Gy for the Monte Carlo summaries and 2.60 Gy for the latent GP posterior. The median within-biopsy reduction was 59.1%, with a median shrinkage ratio of 2.45. Fitted length scales were heterogeneous across biopsies, with median   ℓ ̂ b = 15.35  mm, while nugget fractions were typically small. Cohort standardized residuals were near-centered with conservative spread. In blocked cross-validation, predictive performance on held-out points remained favorable, with median root-mean-square error of 1.99 Gy, median mean absolute error of 1.58 Gy, and median negative log predictive density of 3.28. Among the tested kernels, held-out predictive error favored Matérn ν = 1.5  . CONCLUSION: Along-core dose interpretation after localization uncertainty should use a spatially correlated model rather than separate voxelwise summaries alone. This Gaussian process framework provides a covariance-informed posterior dose representation with held-out internal validation and offers a practical basis for biopsy-level probabilistic quality assurance and future dose-response analyses.

articles.title: Magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction and selected quantitative ultrasound methods for hepatic steatosis: histology-referenced diagnostic performance and longitudinal responsiveness-a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To synthesize histology-referenced diagnostic performance at study-selected thresholds and the longitudinal responsiveness of magnetic resonance imaging proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) and selected quantitative ultrasound methods in adults with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease/metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease. METHODS: Four databases were searched from database inception through July 1, 2026. Sensitivity, specificity, and odds ratios were pooled with 95% confidence intervals using heterogeneity-selected fixed- or random-effects models. Small-study effects were assessed using funnel plots and Begg tests; longitudinal changes were pooled when change-score standard deviations were reported. RESULTS: In total, 44 articles were included: 34 contributed histology-referenced diagnostic data, and 11 were assessed for longitudinal responsiveness, with 1 article contributing to both. At steatosis grade (S) ≥ 1/S ≥ 2/S ≥3, MRI-PDFF sensitivity and specificity was 93.6%/81.5%/83.1% and 87.1%/86.7%/83.2%, respectively; the controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) was 86.8%/81.2%/86.4% and 98.9%/71.0%/64.6%, respectively. The attenuation coefficient/attenuation imaging sensitivity/specificity was 83.2%/98.1%, 86.4%/79.9%, and 99.3%/76.4%, respectively. Ultrasound-guided attenuation parameter and ultrasound-derived fat fraction evidence was limited. Three head-to-head longitudinal studies included 298 participants, of whom only 158 had analyzable change-score data; in these, pooled changes were -4.53 percentage points for MRI-PDFF and -12.71 dB/m for the CAP. Thirty-two of the 34 diagnostic studies were at high-risk of bias from cohort-selected thresholds. Begg tests did not detect significant small-study effects, although their power was very limited in analyses that included only 2 or 3 studies. CONCLUSION: At study-selected thresholds, MRI-PDFF showed balanced sensitivity and specificity across steatosis grades, whereas quantitative ultrasound varied by method, platform, and threshold. These findings support comparative synthesis but do not establish validated cut-offs or superiority of either modality. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: Study-selected thresholds limit clinical translation. MRI-PDFF proton density fat fraction and quantitative ultrasound are complementary, with use depending on clinical purpose, platform, and precision needs.

articles.title: Ordinal uncertainty grading in chest radiograph reports using large language models: a REFINE-aligned feasibility and methodology study.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Radiologists differ in how strongly they hedge. We tested whether large language models can grade linguistic uncertainty in chest radiograph reports on a 0-3 scale and whether aggregate agreement conceals category-specific differences. METHODS: We used 3,927 public chest radiograph reports (Open-I, Indiana University). Three radiologists independently scored 100 reports from 0 (definitive wording) to 3 (extensive ambiguity). Majority vote, with prespecified attending adjudication for seven complete three-way disagreements, formed the reference standard. Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro scored the same reports from a fixed prompt without task-specific training. We measured agreement using Cohen's quadratic weighted kappa (QWK). We also recorded per-score recall, ordinal error, prompt and reference-standard robustness, and comparison with a keyword-counting baseline. We then scored the remaining 3,827 reports with both models. RESULTS: Human pairwise QWK ranged from 0.421 to 0.659. Claude and Gemini had similar aggregate agreement: QWK: 0.807 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.722-0.876] and 0.814 (95% CI, 0.735-0.877), respectively; paired difference: 0.007 (95% CI, -0.062 to 0.079). In this validation sample, Claude identified 5/8 reports exactly as Score 3 and Gemini 1/8; Score-3 precision was 5/11 and 1/3, respectively. Of Gemini's seven exact Score-3 misses, six were assigned the adjacent Score 2 category. Reference-standard sensitivities yielded QWK: 0.810-0.841; prompt-variant pairwise agreement ranged from 0.818 to 0.913; repeat runs were identical for 29/30 Claude and 28/30 Gemini reports. All 3,827 Gemini discovery requests completed successfully, with token accounting recorded for the discovery cohort. CONCLUSION: The approach is workable at the corpus scale, but similar aggregate agreement concealed differences in exact Score-3 classification, largely involving the Score-2/3 boundary. The score reflects wording, not clinical risk, and must not be used for risk triage. Clinical or large-scale use requires external validation enriched for ambiguous cases and prior radiologist calibration. CLINICAL SIGNIFICANCE: These scores may help radiologists audit reporting language and build balanced research evaluation sets, but downstream benefit must be demonstrated rather than assumed.

articles.title: Enterocolitis: a diagnosis in the news that may become more common in the emergency room.
articles.abstract: Foodborne illness affects an estimated 48 million people in the United States each year, and outbreaks peak in the summer. Recalls during the summer of 2026 involved eggs, jalapeños, and frozen blueberries, along with a Cyclospora outbreak traced to iceberg lettuce that caused more than 12,000 illnesses and over 550 hospitalizations. Furthermore, they caused nationwide public anxiety and dominated news headlines. Patients with enteric infection usually reach the emergency department with abdominal pain, and radiologists often read their CT before stool studies return or before anyone suspects infection. This review describes the CT findings of bacterial and parasitic enteritis and colitis. Common features include symmetric segmental or diffuse bowel wall thickening with submucosal edema, mucosal hyperenhancement producing a halo or target pattern, associated fat stranding, engorged mesenteric vessels, and lymphadenopathy. CT also shows complications including toxic megacolon, perforation, and abscess. Recognition of these findings supports timely diagnosis and appropriate management of infectious enterocolitis.

articles.title: Measurement-derived residual-risk verification through four-way k-space partitioning in self-supervised accelerated brain MRI.
articles.abstract: Self-supervised accelerated MRI reconstruction reduces dependence on fully sampled training targets, but it does not inherently provide a separate basis for verifying whether reconstructed image content remains locally consistent with acquired measurements. We developed a measurement-derived verification framework that partitions acquired k-space into four roles: reconstruction input, self-supervised reconstruction-loss evaluation, residual-risk learning, and reserved verification. Residuals from the reserved measurements were transformed into spatial residual-risk targets using density-compensated adjoint projection, probe-based gain normalization, anatomical support weighting, percentile scaling, and logarithmic compression. Using fastMRI brain multicoil data, we evaluated 201 training, 40 calibration, and 40 AXT2 test volumes, comprising 636 test slices and 999,792 sampled pixels. The primary Full-CNN achieved AUPRC 0.8348, mean absolute error 0.0834, Spearman correlation 0.9389, and AUROC 0.9818. The secondary A4-CNN achieved AUPRC 0.8452 with similar scale and rank agreement. MRI-volume intervals achieved at least 90% sampled-location coverage in 39 of 40 test volumes for both predictors. AUPRC declined and MAE increased with fewer reserved measurements and under AXFLAIR sequence shift. Residual-risk maps showed moderate correspondence with fully sampled reference error and differed from the tested predictive-variance measures. The framework provides a measurement-derived verification layer for assessing local residual inconsistency in self-supervised accelerated MRI without requiring fully sampled development targets.

articles.title: Quantitative characterization of spatial frequency-dependent effects of conjugate gradient reconstruction in relation to k-space fill ratio in non-contrast-enhanced ultra-short echo time brain magnetic resonance angiography.
articles.abstract: Ultrashort echo time magnetic resonance angiography (UTE-MRA) with radial sampling is increasingly used for non-contrast cerebrovascular imaging due to its low flow dependence and robustness to susceptibility effects. Reducing the k-space fill ratio to shorten acquisition time may alter the spatial-frequency characteristics of reconstructed images. Conjugate gradient (CG)-based iterative reconstruction compensates for incomplete k-space sampling; however, its frequency-dependent effects remain insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated the spatial-frequency characteristics of CG reconstruction in radial UTE-MRA using the normalized integrated power spectrum (NIPS). Phantom and clinical head UTE-MRA were performed at k-space fill ratios of 2.2%-35.2%, with and without CG reconstruction. NIPS findings were evaluated in relation to signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and acquisition time. The effect of CG reconstruction was more pronounced in the low-frequency range at lower fill ratios, with significant higher NIPS values at 2.2% and 4.4% without CG reconstruction. Furthermore, no significant differences were observed among any combination within the low-frequency band when CG reconstruction was applied at fill ratios of 4.4% or higher (0.051 < P < 0.998). High-frequency NIPS values increased with the k-space fill ratio, indicating greater dependence on physical sampling density. SNR increased with the k-space fill ratio and was not significantly affected by CG reconstruction. In clinical analysis, no statistically significant differences were observed between CG reconstruction at 4.4% and conventional gridding at 8.8% in low- or high-frequency NIPS values within the M1 or M3 segments. Among evaluated conditions, 4.4% with CG reconstruction was selected as a practical acquisition condition.

articles.title: Diffusion tensor imaging and structural MRI reveal early microstructural injury and progressive atrophy of the olfactory bulb in type 1 diabetic rats.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To determine whether diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) can detect early olfactory bulb microstructural abnormalities in streptozotocin (STZ)-induced type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) rats and to investigate their relationship with structural and histopathological changes. METHODS: Control and STZ-induced T1DM rats underwent DTI, high-resolution structural MRI and histological examination at 2 and 12 weeks after model induction. Fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD), axial diffusivity (Da), and radial diffusivity (Dr) were measured in the olfactory nerve layer/glomerular layer/external plexiform layer (ONL/GL/EPL), granule cell layer (GCL), and subependymal zone (SEZ). RESULTS: Compared to the controls, T1DM rats showed decreased FA and increased MD, Da, and Dr. in the ONL/GL/EPL at 2 and 12 weeks after model induction. In the GCL, FA was decreased, whereas Dr. was increased.. No significant diffusion abnormalities were detected in the SEZ. Ultrastructural examination revealed axolemmal disruption, demyelination, reduced axoplasmic content, and axonal vacuolization in the ONL. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) demonstrated olfactory bulb atrophy as early as 2 weeks, initially involving the GCL and SEZ, with more extensive and regionally heterogeneous atrophy at 12 weeks. Nissl staining confirmed structural atrophy, and increased caspase-3 immunoreactivity supported apoptosis-related tissue injury. STZ-induced T1DM causes early, layer-specific olfactory bulb microstructural abnormalities and progressive structural atrophy. CONCLUSION: The differing spatial and temporal distributions of diffusion abnormalities and atrophy suggest that DTI and volumetric MRI capture partially distinct aspects of diabetes-associated olfactory bulb injury. DTI may provide a sensitive, noninvasive approach for detecting early microstructural abnormalities before widespread structural loss develops.

articles.title: Retraining-free multi-task MR image restoration using a pretrained diffusion model with Bayesian optimization.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often requires long scan times, and efforts to shorten scans can lead to image degradation, such as undersampling artifacts, increased noise, and reduced spatial resolution. A restoration framework that can address multiple types of degradation without task-specific retraining would therefore be valuable. In this study, we evaluated whether a pretrained score-based diffusion model combined with Bayesian optimization, termed task guidance design with Bayesian optimization (TGD-BO), could provide retraining-free, multi-task MR image restoration for compressed sensing (CS) reconstruction, super-resolution (SR), and denoising (DN). TGD-BO incorporates data-consistency guidance and gradient guidance into the reverse diffusion process and parameterizes their time-varying strengths using compact low-dimensional B-spline-based guidance schedules. For each task, the schedule was optimized by Bayesian optimization using four paired degraded/reference slices from a single adaptation case, and the resulting task-specific schedule was then applied unchanged to an independent test set. In single-task experiments, TGD-BO improved upon the fixed-guidance diffusion baseline in denoising, compressed-sensing reconstruction, and super-resolution, although the improvement in super-resolution was modest. Compared with task-specific supervised baselines, TGD-BO did not uniformly achieve higher peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) or structural similarity (SSIM); in super-resolution, it showed lower PSNR and SSIM but better perceptual similarity as assessed by learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS). In joint-task experiments, schedules optimized directly for DN + CS and DN + SR yielded numerically better image-quality metrics than applying the corresponding single-task schedules. Sensitivity analyses showed that the selected schedule and test performance were unchanged when 1, 4, or 8 slices from the same adaptation case were used, whereas changing the adaptation case substantially affected test performance. These results suggest the feasibility of adapting a single pretrained diffusion prior across multiple MR image restoration tasks through guidance calibration without task-specific weight retraining, while indicating that robustness to adaptation-case selection and computational cost require further investigation.

Super-Resolution Ultrasound for Lymph Node Evaluation: Diagnostic Value of Static Time-Point Parameters Versus Dynamic Temporal Changes.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate quantitative super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) parameters (static central-to-peripheral ratios and dynamic temporal changes) for differentiating benign and metastatic lymph nodes, and to compare the performance of corresponding predictive models. METHODS: A prospective study included 172 pathologically confirmed lymph nodes (100 benign, 72 metastatic). SRUS was performed to derive density and velocity parameters, with central-to-peripheral ratios and temporal changes calculated. Static and dynamic models were constructed using univariate analysis, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and logistic regression. Model performance was assessed by cross-validation, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration, decision curve analysis, and clinical impact curve. RESULTS: Metastatic lymph nodes showed significantly lower central-to-peripheral ratios of density and velocity parameters but higher relative temporal changes in density SD and velocity SD compared with benign nodes (all P < .05). The static time-point model retained 2 SRUS variables (Mean.Density_C_P_T2, Max.Density_C_P_T3), yielding a full-sample AUC of 0.8607. The temporal change model included 2 dynamic parameters (Velocity SD change from T1 to T2, Mean density change from T2 to T3) and achieved a higher AUC of 0.8715, with better accuracy, specificity, and model fit. Both models showed favorable calibration and clinical net benefit. CONCLUSION: Quantitative SRUS parameters effectively reflect pathological angiogenesis in metastatic lymph nodes. The temporal change model provides superior diagnostic performance over the static time-point model and may serve as a reliable noninvasive tool for distinguishing benign from metastatic lymph nodes.

articles.title: Evaluation of Microvascular Flow Characteristics of Hepatic Hemangiomas: A Prospective Comparison of Ultra-Micro Angiography With Conventional Doppler and the Effects of Lesion Depth, Size, and Steatosis.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare ultra-micro angiography (UMA) modalities-color (cUMA), power (pUMA), and subtraction UMA (sUMA)-with conventional color Doppler (CD) and power Doppler (PD) in hepatic hemangiomas, and to identify factors limiting flow detectability, including lesion depth, size, and steatosis. METHODS: In this prospective single-center study, hemangiomas confirmed by contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging underwent B-mode ultrasound, CD, PD, and 3 UMA modes. Vascularity was graded with the Adler scale (0-3), and the vascular index measured for each modality. Steatosis was graded visually and quantified by ultrasound attenuation (USAT). Groups with and without flow were compared with the Mann-Whitney U test; predictors of detectability were assessed by logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis. RESULTS: Of 138 hemangiomas in 81 patients, 124 were analyzed; flow was detected in 89 (71.8%). Flow-positive hemangiomas were shallower (44.67 versus 87.06 mm) and larger (29.53 versus 17.89 mm; p < .001 for both). Depth was the strongest predictor (area under the ROC curve 0.904; cutoff 59 mm), followed by size (0.710) and USAT (0.612); moderate and severe steatosis (grades 2 and 3) independently reduced detection (p ≤ .045). Adler grade 2 or higher was present in 65-73% of hemangiomas on UMA versus 21-24% on conventional Doppler (p < .001). Strip rim (30.3%) and peripheral dot-like (23.6%) patterns predominated; interobserver agreement was good (κ = 0.748). CONCLUSIONS: UMA outperforms conventional Doppler in hepatic hemangiomas; depth, small size, and moderate-to-severe steatosis limit signal detection, and peripheral microvascular patterns parallel the globular enhancement on computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

articles.title: Comparative reasoning in radiology artificial intelligence: longitudinal and reference-case approaches.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in radiology remains predominantly examination-centric, whereas clinical interpretation frequently depends on comparison across time or with relevant prior cases. This narrative review examines comparative reasoning in radiology AI through two related but clinically distinct forms: longitudinal reasoning, which compares examinations from the same patient over time, and reference-case reasoning, which uses clinically analogous cases from other patients to support interpretation. We propose a capability hierarchy that distinguishes simple access to comparative information from higher-level capabilities, including selection of relevant historical context, anatomical and lesion-level correspondence, characterization of interval change, temporal-state interpretation, multi-interval trajectory reasoning, and entity-specific assessment of clinical similarity. This distinction matters because providing prior examinations or retrieving visually similar cases does not itself demonstrate meaningful comparative reasoning. We review developments in prior-examination selection, registration, lesion tracking, temporal vision-language modeling, treatment-response assessment, analogous-case retrieval, and longitudinal report generation. Particular emphasis is placed on evaluation strategies that determine whether model performance depends appropriately on clinically relevant comparative information rather than on additional input volume, global image similarity, acquisition characteristics, or other shortcuts. Key challenges include incorrect prior selection, lesion mismatching, temporal inconsistency, clinically irrelevant reference-case retrieval, data leakage, misleading comparative language, and propagation of historical errors. Future progress will require models that preserve entity identity, reason coherently across multi-visit imaging histories, identify clinically informative reference cases, and demonstrate benefit under realistic clinical conditions. Comparative reasoning is therefore a necessary step in the transition from examination-level toward patient-level radiology AI.
